title: Total Recall at What Cost? Benchmarking the Serving Cost of Agentic Memory Systems

visual_explainer.blocker: A paper-specific GPT Image invocation on 2026-08-13 failed at the image-tool level before a render was returned. Earlier same-run isolated attempts for MESA and MAP-Graph also failed paper identity/grounding. The image tool required no further retries in this request; no visual was published.

analysis.tldr: This paper turns serving cost into a first-class agent-memory benchmark and shows that dedicated memory is not automatically cheaper than resending history: break-even depends strongly on architecture, backbone, message size, and conversation length, with no system dominating both cost and accuracy.
analysis.problem: Memory systems are often justified by avoiding ever-growing full-history prompts, but their own ingest, retrieval, reflection, and answer pipelines consume model calls. Prior evaluations rarely measure those costs under matched systems/backbones or ask when memory actually pays back its overhead.
analysis.core_idea: Replay identical conversations through Mem0, Hindsight, Mastra Observational Memory, a ten-turn rolling window, and full-history prompting. Instrument billed input across ingest/retrieval/answer stages, fit a depth×message-size cost surface, compute sustained break-even against full history from measured per-turn cost, and pair each configuration with LoCoMo answer accuracy.

memory_design.write: The benchmark leaves each system's ingest pipeline intact and meters its billed model input, including fact extraction or reflection/consolidation when the implementation triggers it.
memory_design.organize: Memory representations are not standardized; the benchmark intentionally spans flat fact extraction, retain/recall/reflect, and observer/reflector designs while measuring their serving behavior under matched configurations.
memory_design.read: Each system retrieves from its native memory and answers under the benchmark backbone; rolling-window and full-history strategies provide transparent cost references.
memory_design.update_forget: The paper evaluates each implementation's native ingest/consolidation behavior rather than proposing a new lifecycle policy.

compared_to: Full-transcript resubmission as the cost ceiling
A fixed ten-turn rolling window as the cheap non-persistent floor
Mem0, Hindsight, and Mastra Observational Memory under common backbone/reasoning settings
analysis.evidence: A separable depth/message-size regression predicts the two window baselines with 2.9–6.5% held-out error but misses memory systems by 18–69%, showing internal memory behavior drives cost. Across measured 400-turn workloads, sustained break-even against full history spans Mastra OM 0–86 turns, Mem0 0–342, and Hindsight 60–never. At 400 turns full history can cost up to 12.7× a memory system after break-even, while Hindsight can still cost up to 3.3× full history in small-message cases. Accuracy across configurations spans about 21–54%; no system dominates both axes.
analysis.why_it_matters: This challenges a common systems premise: retrieval memory is not economically justified merely because it sends fewer answer-time history tokens. Architecture-specific maintenance work and serving-stack choice can move the break-even point by hundreds of turns, so cost must be measured as an end-to-end lifecycle property.
limitations: The cost grid uses synthetic dialogues whose fact density may not reproduce real ingest/consolidation behavior.
Accuracy is evaluated on one stratified LoCoMo subset, so joint cost-quality conclusions may not transfer to task-oriented agents.
The fitted cost model is descriptive and generalizes poorly for the memory systems; it should not be extrapolated mechanistically.
Hindsight's ingest backbone was not controlled across benchmark cells, so its cross-backbone/reasoning comparisons are explicitly invalid.
Provider routing/caching variance and serving-stack token-count mismatches affect observed costs.
